records.why: The phases as written add up to about 160 minutes: Observe 40 + 15, Model Building 20 + 25 + 10, plus Predict, Explain and Driving Question Board, but the lesson has 3 x 40 = 120 minutes. records.group_headline: Lesson 8 phases added up to about 160 minutes in a 120-minute slot; trimmed so they fit (presentations 3+1 min per group, shorter Kericho recalculation, quicker class diagram)

records.old: Part 1 (about 40 minutes): project presentations. records.why: Lesson 5 promises that a rectangular base 'will be tested in Lesson 6 problems', and the unit content lists square and rectangular bases, but every pyramid example was square. Problem 4 uses similar rectangles (both sides halve): A1 = 600, A2 = 150, sqrt(600 x 150) = sqrt(90,000) = 300, V = 1/3 x 24 x 1,050 = 8,400 cm³ = 8.4 L. I checked it a second way: large pyramid height 48 cm gives 1/3 x 600 x 48 = 9,600; small pyramid 1/3 x 150 x 24 = 1,200; 9,600 - 1,200 = 8,400. Mass 8.4 x 0.75 = 6.3 kg.
records.old: divide the volume of drum A (83,160 cm³) by it to find how many cups fill the drum.
records.new: divide the volume of drum A (83,160 cm³) by it to find how many cups fill the drum. Early finishers (and the whole class if time allows) do Problem 4: a maize store shaped as a frustum of a rectangular pyramid, top 30 cm by 20 cm, bottom 15 cm by 10 cm, height 24 cm; find its capacity in litres with the frustum-of-a-pyramid formula and the mass of maize it holds at 0.75 kg per litre.
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 curriculum design (content list for this sub-strand as given in the unit data: frustums of pyramids with square and rectangular bases); no KICD source for Essential Mathematics was available to check against
records.group_headline: KICD asks for frustums of pyramids with square AND rectangular bases, but no lesson or the final task used a rectangular base; added one rectangular-base problem in Lesson 6, in the Lesson 8 written activity and in the Final Explanation

records.why: Knock-on: gives teachers the worked answer and the second-method check for Problem 4.
records.old: (75 L, which is less than 80.52 L, so it still fits.)
records.new: (75 L, which is less than 80.52 L, so it still fits.) Problem 4 answer: A1 = 600 cm², A2 = 150 cm², sqrt(A1 A2) = 300 cm², V = 1/3 x 24 x (600 + 150 + 300) = 8,400 cm³ = 8.4 L, and 8.4 x 0.75 = 6.3 kg of maize. Check by large-minus-small: large pyramid (height 48 cm) 1/3 x 600 x 48 = 9,600 cm³, small pyramid (height 24 cm) 1/3 x 150 x 24 = 1,200 cm³, and 9,600 - 1,200 = 8,400 cm³. The formula still works for a rectangular base because the top and bottom faces of a frustum are always the same shape (here both sides halve).

records.why: Knock-on: item (d) copied the Lesson 5 practice bin (40/20/30, 28 L, 21 kg), so it tested memory of a worked example; it now uses a new rectangular-base frustum. Mass 21 x 0.75 = 15.75 kg.

records.why: Lesson 7, Lesson 8 and the Final Explanation presented '5-10%' as a finding although handmade cardboard models can easily be further off; teachers and learners would be marking real data against a number nobody measured. Now the class records its own range and treats 5-10% only as a typical expectation.
records.old: discuss why measured values differ by about 5-10%, for example
records.new: discuss why measured values usually differ from calculated ones (careful card models are often within about 10%, but the class's own results decide), for example
records.group_headline: The project lessons announced a 5-10% error before anyone had measured anything; the plan now uses the class's own results

records.why: Knock-on: the teacher asks about the real class range.
records.old: Pose the key challenge: 'Our errors are mostly within 5 to 10 percent. What does that tell you about whether the formulas are trustworthy?'
records.new: Pose the key challenge using the class table: 'Our errors range from ___ to ___ percent. What does that tell you about whether the formulas are trustworthy?' Careful models are often within about 10 percent; if the class range is wider, treat that as evidence to investigate, not as a failure.

records.why: Knock-on: learners record their own range instead of copying a pre-written one.

records.new: 'Calculated vs measured: our errors were ___ % to ___ %, caused by (our own causes, for example card thickness, seams, spills)'

records.why: Drawing and cutting nets for three models, assembling, measuring, calculating and testing, then explaining error, the Driving Question Board and the model are far more than 80 minutes for 30 learners sharing scissors. Preparing nets as homework is the most practical fix; teachers know whether learners can get card at home and may prefer to supply it.
records.old: each group draws nets on cereal-box cardboard and builds a cone
records.new: each group brings the nets it drew and cut out at home after Lesson 6 (or draws them quickly in class on cereal-box cardboard) and builds a cone
records.group_headline: Building, measuring, calculating and testing three models cannot fit in 80 minutes; nets are now prepared as homework after Lesson 6 and a time guide is added

records.why: Knock-on: a time guide that adds to 80 (8 + 38 + 14 + 8 + 12; 15 + 10 + 13 = 38); a practical tip (a card cone cannot be filled without a stand) and an inclusion option.
records.old: Support groups who struggle to make a frustum of a pyramid by showing four trapezium faces on a net, but do not provide the dimensions.
records.new: Support groups who struggle to make a frustum of a pyramid by showing four trapezium faces on a net, but do not provide the dimensions. Time guide for the 80 minutes: Predict 8, Observe 38 (assemble 15, measure and calculate 10, fill and read 13), Explain 14, Driving Question Board 8, Model Building 12. A cone cannot stand on its point: stand it in a cup of sand or a ring of card before filling. Learners who find cutting or pouring difficult can take the measuring, calculating or photographing role, and can show understanding with an oral explanation or a labelled sketch.

records.why: The sentence was confusing ('full-size version'): the 30 x 30 x 40 cm pyramid already holds 12 L and its cuboid 36 L, which is a lot of sand or water for every group in a large class. Smaller models give the same 3 : 1 result, so the check now says so. 30 x 30 x 40 = 36,000 cm³; 36,000 / 3 = 12,000 cm³.
records.old: to check it is about 12 L in the full-size version or scaled to model capacity; record the ratio.
records.new: to check it is about 12 L (12,000 mL) for the 30 cm x 30 cm x 40 cm models, or one third of the cuboid's measured volume if your school has smaller models (any size works because the ratio stays 3 : 1); record the ratio.

records.why: Lesson 4 holds measuring, similar triangles, a full algebraic derivation, a comparison table, the Driving Question Board and the class model in 80 minutes. The difference-of-cubes factorisation may be new to Essential Mathematics learners, so teachers now have a way to shorten it without losing the numerical check (1/3 x 22/7 x 60 x 931 = 58,520).
records.old: If learners struggle, show the pattern with numbers (441, 294, 196) before the letters.
records.new: If learners struggle, show the pattern with numbers (441, 294, 196) before the letters. If learners have not yet met the difference of cubes, skip the factorising in Step 3: give the formula and verify it numerically on bucket C (both methods give 58,520 cm³); this also saves time in a full lesson.

records.why: The small pyramid is the part that was removed, so it cannot fit 'at the top of the removed part'. In this bin the wide 60 cm side is the top, so the 30 cm pyramid (height 40 cm) fits beneath the narrow end, giving a large pyramid of height 40 + 40 = 80 cm, as the calculations in the same phase use.
records.old: fits at the top of the removed part.
records.new: fits under the narrow 30 cm end of the frustum to complete the large pyramid (side 60 cm, height 80 cm).

records.why: The note called 30 x 24 = 720 a mistake, but 720 is the correct Rr term used in the answer (900 + 720 + 576 = 2,196). Checked: (30 + 24)² = 2,916, which would be the wrong total.
records.old: squaring incorrectly (e.g. 30 x 24 = 720 mistaken)
records.new: leaving out the Rr term (30 x 24 = 720 is correct and must be included) or using (R + r)² instead of R² + Rr + r²

records.why: The sub-strand had no language support for English learners. Teacher decision: please check these Kiswahili terms with a Kiswahili or mathematics teacher (I could not verify them), and add terms for capacity and frustum, which I left out because I was not certain of the standard words.
records.old: Ensure learners know that h is the vertical height.
records.new: Ensure learners know that h is the vertical height. Language support for English learners: put key words on the word wall with a Kiswahili partner term, for example ujazo (volume), koni (cone), silinda (cylinder), piramidi (pyramid), kipenyo (diameter), nusu kipenyo (radius), urefu (height), and let learners explain an idea to a partner in Kiswahili or their home language before they write it in English.

records.why: The three level descriptors now name the CBE levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches Expectations) so teachers see how they map to KICD levels. Wording of each descriptor is unchanged.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: All volumes, capacities, ratios and conversions are correct, use pi = 22/7, and include correct units with litres to 2 decimal places for the Kericho containers.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Most calculations are correct, with one or two small slips in arithmetic or units that do not change the conclusion.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Several calculations or conversions are incorrect, or units are missing, so the conclusions are not supported.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Chooses the correct formula for each solid and uses the large-minus-small method and similar triangles accurately, showing the cone-cylinder and pyramid-cuboid one-third relationships.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Uses the correct formulas in most cases but the working for similar triangles or large-minus-small is partly incomplete.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Uses wrong formulas or cannot show how a frustum relates to a cone or pyramid.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Clearly explains that the containers differ in capacity because their shape differs, uses 27.72 L, 58.52 L and 83.16 L, and answers Mr. Kiprop's question with the tapering reasoning.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains that shape matters and quotes the capacities, but the reasoning about tapering is general or incomplete.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: States that the containers differ without a mathematical explanation or with incorrect numbers.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Uses evidence from the pouring and model investigations, explains percentage error and its causes, and describes a clear process for designing a frustum of a required capacity.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Mentions evidence and at least one cause of error, and gives a partial design process.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Gives little evidence from the investigations and no clear explanation of error or design.

value.criterion: Communication and usefulness of volume and capacity
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Writes clear, well-organised steps in sensible language and gives well-chosen Kenyan examples that show why volume and capacity are useful.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Writing is mostly clear and gives one or two examples of usefulness.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Writing is hard to follow and gives no examples of why volume and capacity are useful.

records.why: The CBE rubric has four levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations), but the data contract allows only three level fields, so Below Expectations cannot be printed in the Final Explanation rubric. Suggestion: teachers treat any work below the Approaches descriptor as Below Expectations, or the partner contract is extended.

The three supporting phenomena (mandazi cone bag versus frustum cup, Lake Turkana cistern in jerricans, Nairobi pyramid display stand filled with sand) are listed in the unit but none appears in any lesson, so they do not support the anchor visibly. Suggestion: use the display stand as the context for Lesson 3 (sand test), the cistern in Lesson 6 (litres to 20 L jerricans), and the mandazi bag as a Lesson 4 or 7 extension (same slant height does not mean the same volume), or remove them from the unit.

No KICD source for Essential Mathematics is available here: the Mathematics PDF in data/raw/curriculum_pdfs is the Core Mathematics design and has no Volume and Capacity sub-strand 2.7 (its 'Volume of Solids' sub-strand is different). KICD wording, strand and sub-strand numbering, key inquiry question, competencies and values could not be checked and were left unchanged. Teachers should compare them with the Essential Mathematics design. Content outcomes (a to e) are each taught and assessed in Lesson 8.
